title: How the hell are you guys actually generating usable 2D sprite sheets? Standard image generators absolutely suck for this.
author: BeDevForLife
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I’m working on a 2D game and decided to try using AI for the character assets and animations. I started by using standard image generators (ChatGPT, Midjourney, etc.) to prompt for "2D sprite sheets," and honestly... it sucks.

The frames look like completely different characters; there’s no concept of actual motion consistency, the proportions morph between frames, and cleaning up backgrounds because they can't output true transparency is a nightmare. I’m spending more time fixing the "slop" than I would just doing it manually.

I know people are making actual games here, so what is the *real* workflow right now? Thanks!

comments.author: Immediate_Hornet8273
comments.body: Pixellab.ai I generate my characters there and then created custom python apps to format the downloaded gif package into sprite sheets. Then I use Upscayl to 4x the sheet for an “HD” look. This allows the player to choose from a pixel art style or a more smooth HD effect as a video option. I also created a python app that can generate cosmetic item art overlays from the original flat image and allow you to warp and reposition the item for each frame, then exports a packaged sprite sheet for the item overlay.

comments.author: Virtue_Driven
comments.body:
use the spritesheets to create subassets, then use those subassets as ref images.

So instead of giving the whole sheet, screenshot just the pose that's closest to what you want and modify it to be exactly what you want in your starting frame

As far as morphing between frames goes, look up De-Ropeing. takes a lots of manual time and you have to inspect frames individually so hopefully this improves with time.

comments.author: DatabaseNearby5
comments.body:
I managed to get around a 80-90% success rate generating one move at a time. Iterating on the prompts + am LLM scoring pass + a small pipeline of other tools that runs after the generation (for instance if one of the frames needs to move to left or right thats something you can have done automatically).

That said the 10-20% of the time it does fail is generally on the same kind of pose… anything where an arm or leg is extended tends to bleed between frames quite often

For models I was on Nanobanana for a while, but the  latest OpenAI models are much better at generating transparent backgrounds and much cheaper for smaller images

replies.author: xcdesz
replies.body: I did this just last week.  Vibe coded an app using to take a portrait of a character, used Krea image edit model/lora (via comfy rest api) to convert to a side view of the character on a white background, erased the white using a bg removal workflow, used a minimax h3 prompt to animate a few seconds of walking / idle, extracted frames of the video to use as the animation frames (8 frames for 1 animation).  Tested it out in a sandbox platform harness and it worked relatively smoothly.  Biggest challenge was the bg removal isnt perfect and had to manually edit some frames.  App had a pixel editor for that part.  Non-pixelated graphics, the video and image gen purely on local hardware.

comments.author: Ill-Ant-9489
comments.body:
Sprite sheets drift because text to image re-rolls the character from scratch every prompt, so the face and proportions wander frame to frame. What holds is locking one character first, then posing that locked identity instead of re-prompting. Either edit a single reference into each pose so the same character carries over, or train a small character LoRA so the proportions stop moving.

None of this outputs true transparency though, that stays a background removal pass after, and walk cycles need more frames than a jump, so plan the pose list first.

The locking part is what my app handles, it poses one reference into the facings a sheet needs and culls the frames where the face slips, https://github.com/perfectgf/lora-dataset-studio (mine). Fixed turnaround or actual animation frames?

I use combination of ChatGPT and Claude for my game. Claude directs and ChatGPT draws. They talk to each other over a local chat.

replies.author: BeDevForLife
replies.body: can you explain more, please

replies.author: snobesque
replies.body: I explain Claude what I want to get. Claude writes prompts and creates wireframes. Then a task is passed to ChatGPT that draws sprite sheets and returns results back to Claude. Claude checks, he even can make minor corrections himself like aligning the characters between frames. If result from ChatGPT is bad we fix the prompt and go for the next iteration.

comments.author: CmdrCallandra

Hi there, this is the reason why I began working on my own tool. Premise is, it needs to be 100% local and from licenses permissable for commercial use (like MIT).

The workflow right now for 2D is still based around the 3D base, i. e. Generate model and animations first, then 2D / pixel art those. Feel free to give input on what you think is missing, am keen to bring in as many use cases around asset generation that I can.

https://github.com/SifuInTheShell/Effigy

Claude generates options from openai and gemini and I pick the best one in an artboard picker app it built for me. I can comment back and ask for another set or specific tweaks as well.
